checks.name: Ritter dry-bed dam break
checks.threshold: relative L2 0.305% < 5%, h(dam) error 0.94% < 5%, front lag 18.3% in [0%, 25%)
checks.note: The front lag is expected and is documented, not a defect: a monotone second-order scheme cannot resolve the infinite-gradient tip where depth reaches zero. It must never LEAD the analytical front, which would mean the wave is arriving too early.

checks.name: Stoker wet-bed dam break
checks.note: The wet-bed case is the one that matters for a real reach, where the flood runs onto an existing river rather than a dry bed. It produces a genuine shock, so it tests the HLLC solver rather than only the rarefaction.

checks.name: Lake at rest over irregular bed (well-balancedness)
checks.note: Over a bed with 118 m of relief. A non-well-balanced scheme produces velocities of order sqrt(g*dz) here, i.e. several m/s of flow that does not exist.

checks.name: Mass conservation, no wet/dry front
checks.note: Water is given an initial momentum so it sloshes against the walls; a static test would pass trivially. Every cell stays wet throughout, so this measures the flux scheme alone.

checks.name: Wet/dry mass budget (measured cost of drying)
checks.note: This is not a conservation failure to be fixed; it is the price of a wet/dry treatment, quantified. The number is reported alongside every simulation so a reviewer can see what it cost on their own case.

checks.name: Grid convergence (Ritter)
checks.threshold: observed order 0.91 > 0.8 and error decreases with dx
checks.note: Second order is not attainable on a discontinuous solution; roughly first order in L1 is the expected and correct result at a shock.

checks.name: Frictional dam break (front retardation)
checks.threshold: rough front 1175 m < frictionless 1318 m <= Ritter 1396 m
checks.note: The Dressler/Whitham line is a first-order asymptotic estimate shown for orientation, not a precision benchmark. The assertion being tested is the ordering: friction must retard the front, and the frictionless front must never outrun Ritter.

checks.name: Thacker parabolic bowl (moving shoreline)
checks.note: Thacker, W.C. (1981). Some exact solutions to the nonlinear shallow-water wave equations. J. Fluid Mech. 107, 499-508. Pass criterion: the oscillation period. The NSE of the velocity series (Nash, J.E. & Sutcliffe, J.V. (1970). River flow forecasting through conceptual models part I. J. Hydrology 10(3), 282-290.) is reported as a descriptive score only; amplitude damping lowers it without indicating a momentum error.

checks.name: SPH: Ritter dry-bed dam break
checks.threshold: relative L2 7.517% < 8%, h(dam) error 10.03% < 5%, front lag 56.5% >= 0 (never leads)
checks.note: The SPH front lags further than the finite-volume front because the kernel sum under-counts depth within one smoothing length of a free surface. It lags; it never leads, which is the direction that matters for warning time.

checks.name: SPH: Stoker wet-bed dam break
checks.note: The shock is captured by Monaghan artificial viscosity rather than by a Riemann solver, which is what makes this an independent check on the finite-volume result rather than the same numerics twice.

checks.name: SPH: exact volume and momentum conservation
checks.threshold: volume error 0.0e+00 < 1e-12, net momentum 2.2e-16 of carried < 1e-10
checks.note: A symmetric hump collapses into two waves moving in opposite directions; the net momentum must stay zero. This is the test that proves the pair forces really are equal and opposite — and that the kernel is actually evaluated.

checks.name: SPH: lake at rest (measured, not exact)
checks.note: Unlike FloodGuard-SWE, which is well-balanced to round-off, SPH balances the kernel depth gradient against the DEM bed slope only approximately. This measures the residual. It is orders of magnitude below dam-break flow speeds, but it is why FloodGuard-SWE, not SPH, is the primary engine for the KPIs.

checks.name: SPH: convergence under particle refinement
checks.note: SPH at a fixed smoothing-length-to-spacing ratio converges slowly — the kernel smoothing error does not vanish with spacing alone. The order is reported, not dressed up: it is well below the finite-volume solver's.
